title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Ad secundum et tertium: consequent hardening vs eternal will not to soften
pass_a_gloss: To the second and third: When Augustine bids us believe that his evil deserts are not absent, or preceded, whom God permits to be hardened, he does not speak of that eternal will of not-having-mercy, of not-softening, which contains reprobation itself, but of that hardening in which the sinner justly forsaken by God contracts as it were a certain stony hardness; which we by no means deny to be the wage of preceding sins. But here it is needful to weigh, that howsoever this hardening, considered as increased and advanced, as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from the demerit of preceding sins, yet that first permissive hardening, which is considered as the mere negation of softening on God's part, cannot arise from the same foresighted demerit. For that the will of not-having-mercy, of not-softening, considered in God, should be born from foresight of hardening considered in man, would be equally absurd as if someone said that that daylight of the sun absent among the Cimmerians arises from the preceding long darkening of the air.
pass_b_english: To the second and third: when Augustine bids us believe evil deserts are not absent — or went before — in him whom God permits to be hardened, he is not speaking of that eternal will not to have mercy, not to soften, which contains reprobation itself. He means the hardening in which the sinner, justly forsaken by God, contracts a kind of stony hardness — and we do not deny that is the wage of preceding sins. Weigh this: however much that hardening, taken as increased and advanced as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from demerit of preceding sins, the first permissive hardening — mere negation of softening on God's part — cannot arise from that same foresighted demerit. To say God's will not to have mercy, not to soften, is born from foresight of human hardening would be as absurd as saying the sun's daylight, absent among the Cimmerians, arises from the air's long prior darkening.
source_text: Ad secundum et tertium: Quando Augustinus jubet nos credere ejus mala merita non abesse, aut praecessisse, quem Deus indurari permittit, non loquitur de illa aeterna voluntate non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, quae ipsam reprobationem continet, sed de ea obduratione in qua peccator a Deo juste derelictus quasi lapideam quandam duritiem contrahit; quam esse praecedentium peccatorum mercedem haud negamus. Sed hic perpendere oportet, utcunque haec obduratio, quae aucta et provecta consideratur, ut mala dispositio hominis indurati, ex demerito praecedentium peccatorum oriatur, tamen illa prima induratio permissiva, quae consideratur ut sola negatio emollitionis ex parte Dei, non potest oriri ex eodem praeviso demerito. Nam voluntatem non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, in Deo consideratam nasci ex praevisione obdurationis in homine consideratam, aeque absurdum esset ac si quis dixerit diluculum illud solis absentem apud Cimmerios oriri ex praeeunte diuturna obtenebratione aeris.
